title: GPT, start to finish
subtitle: The whole pipeline on a real tiny GPT: tokens → vectors → attention → probabilities → loop

segments.text: Mia gives her red ball to Tom. Now Tom has the... what? This tiny GPT, a model that predicts the next word, says red. It's 87 percent sure. Nobody told it the rules.
segments.scene: The prompt 'mia has a red ball. tom has a blue kite. mia gives the ball to tom. now tom has the ___' appears line by line; the blank fills with 'red' and an 87% badge.

segments.text: And this model is tiny. It has three layers and 170 thousand parameters, the numbers it learns. It was trained for 80 seconds on an ordinary CPU. That's about a million times smaller than GPT-3.

segments.text: Step four: the layers. Attention moves information between tokens. Then a small MLP, a simple neural network, works on each token alone. Each one adds its result onto the token's vector, the running list of numbers for that token. That running total is called the residual stream. One attention plus one MLP make a layer, and this model stacks three.

segments.text: Step five: turn that into a prediction. The final vector is compared with all 256 tokens it knows, giving each one a score. Then softmax turns the scores into probabilities, chances that add up to one. Red gets 87 percent, white 6, purple 5, and the rest get crumbs.

segments.text: Step six: pick and repeat. Take the top pick, add it to the end, and run it again. Out comes red, then ball, a period, a newline, and once upon a time. Always taking the top pick is called greedy. Rolling weighted dice, so likely tokens come up more often, is called sampling.

title: Tokens: how a model reads
subtitle: Byte-pair encoding, merge by merge, with TinyGPT's real 256-token vocab

segments.text: Models can't read letters. They only take in numbers. So how does a word like Wednesday get in? The answer is tokens, numbered chunks of text.
segments.scene: The word 'wednesday' in big letters above a box labelled 'the model — only eats numbers', with an arrow and '[ ?, ?, ? ]' between them.

objects.label: the word "wednesday"
TinyGPT only accepts integer token ids (0–255)

segments.text: The simplest trick is to give each character its own number. Our model starts with 35 base symbols. There are 26 letters, plus a space and a newline, which starts a new line. Then come six punctuation marks, and an unknown token for anything else.
segments.scene: A grid of the 35 base tokens with their ids: <unk> (0), newline (1), space (2), a–z (3–28), and . , ? ! : ' (29–34).

objects.label: token 0: <unk> (unknown character)
token 1: newline
token 2: space
tokens 3–28: the letters a–z

segments.text: But then Wednesday, with the space in front of it, costs ten tokens. And the model has to re-spell every common word from scratch, letter by letter. That's slow and wasteful.
segments.scene: ' wednesday' (with its leading space, shown as ␣) split into 10 single-character chips with ids 2, 25, 7, 6, 16, 7, 21, 6, 3, 27. Flash: '10 tokens for one word?!'

segments.text: A method called byte-pair encoding fixes this. It builds bigger tokens by merging pairs that often appear together. First, chop the text it learns from into words. Each word keeps the space in front of it. Merges never cross from one word into the next.
segments.scene: The corpus snippet 'tom has a blue boat. tom gives' is split into word pieces (tom · ␣has · ␣a · ␣blue · ␣boat · . · ␣tom · ␣gives), with yellow separators: merges never cross a word boundary.

pre-token " boat": merges only happen inside it
pre-token ".": merges only happen inside it
pre-token " tom": merges only happen inside it
pre-token " gives": merges only happen inside it
BPE splits text into words first (leading space attached); merges never cross words

segments.text: Next, count every pair of neighbors inside those words, meaning two symbols side by side. It counts across the first 400 thousand characters of text. The winner is space t, a space followed by the letter t, found 13,558 times. Merge it into a brand new token, and repeat.

segments.text: Repeat that 221 times. You end up with the 35 base symbols plus 221 new tokens. That's a vocabulary of exactly 256 tokens, the full set it knows.

segments.text: Now let's use the rules to turn new text, like Wednesday, into tokens. Start from single characters, and replay the merges in the order they were learned. Space w merges first, then a y, then e d. The lowest rule number always goes first.

segments.text: Notice that these splits ignore grammar. The piece 'esday' exists because Tuesday and Wednesday both end with it. Jumping becomes space, j, um, p, ing, not jump plus ing. And the model never sees inside a token, only its ID number.
segments.scene: Examples: ' tuesday' → ␣t · u · esday (shares 'esday', id 202, with wednesday); ' jumping' → ␣ · j · um · p · ing.

segments.text: Words that show up a lot get a token all to themselves. Space red, the word red with its space, is just ID 157, one single chunk.

segments.text: There's one catch. This model's tiny world of stories is all lowercase, so a capital W becomes the unknown token. Most real tokenizers, the tools that do this chopping, start from the 256 possible bytes instead. All text on a computer is stored as bytes, so nothing is ever unknown.
segments.scene: 'Wednesday' with a capital W encodes as <unk> (id 0) · ed · n · esday: TinyGPT's vocab is lowercase only. Note: most real tokenizers start from the 256 possible bytes, so nothing is ever unknown.

segments.text: So how big do vocabularies get? Our vocab has 256 entries. GPT-2 had 50,257. Newer models go past 100 thousand. It's the same algorithm, just with a bigger table.
segments.scene: Vocab-size bars to scale: TinyGPT 256 (a sliver), GPT-2 50,257, newer LLMs drawn at 100,000 with an arrow for 'and up'. Flash: 'same algorithm, bigger table'.

segments.text: A bigger vocab means fewer tokens per sentence. But it means a bigger embedding table, with a row of numbers for each token. It's a knob you'll get to turn when you build your own. So tokens are numbered chunks of text.
segments.scene: Trade-off: bigger vocab → fewer tokens per sentence but a bigger embedding table (TinyGPT 256×64 = 16,384 numbers; GPT-2 50,257×768 = 38.6 million).

title: Embeddings: words as directions
subtitle: The lookup table that turns token ids into 64 numbers, and the meaning hiding in them

segments.text: To this model, the word red is just token 157, a numbered chunk of text. That number is just a row in a table. So how does a number come to mean anything? The answer is embeddings.
segments.scene: A big token chip '␣red' with its id 157 underneath and the question 'what does 157 mean?'.

objects.label: token " red" has id 157 in the 256-token vocabulary

segments.text: The very first step is a lookup table. It has 256 rows, one for each token, with 64 numbers in each row. Orange cells are positive, blue ones negative. Token 157 simply grabs row 157. That row is its embedding, the list of numbers that stands for the token.
segments.scene: The real 256×64 embedding table as a heatmap (orange positive, blue negative). Row 157 is outlined and slides out as a strip of 64 cells; its first values are -0.17, -0.14, -0.18, +0.07 … -0.19.

objects.label: token " red" has id 157 in the 256-token vocabulary
the real token-embedding table: 256 rows × 64 columns = 16,384 learned numbers
embedding of " red" (row 157): 64 numbers from -0.28 to +0.28, length 1.18

segments.text: All 16,384 numbers in this table started as random noise. And the same table is reused at the very end, to score every possible next token. So training, the model's learning process, pulls tokens that fit the same slots toward similar rows. In other words, tokens that fill the same spot in a sentence, like two colors, get similar numbers.
segments.scene: Same view; captions: 'started random → shaped by training' and 'reused at the end to score every next token (weight tying)'. The table holds 16,384 of the model's 170,560 parameters.

objects.label: token " red" has id 157 in the 256-token vocabulary
the real token-embedding table: 256 rows × 64 columns = 16,384 learned numbers
embedding of " red" (row 157): 64 numbers from -0.28 to +0.28, length 1.18
weight tying: logits = final vector · every row of this same embedding table

segments.text: No single number means red. Think of the whole row as an arrow: what matters is the direction it points. Purple points almost the same way. We compare directions with cosine similarity, which measures how well two arrows line up. One means same way, zero means unrelated.
segments.scene: Toy 2-D picture: arrows for ' red' and ' purple' point almost the same way, ' tom' points elsewhere. Text: cosine similarity = how aligned two arrows are (+1 same way, 0 unrelated, −1 opposite).

objects.label: toy 2-D illustration of embedding directions (not real values)
cosine similarity: +1 same direction, 0 unrelated, −1 opposite

segments.text: Now the real thing. Red's nearest neighbours are the tokens whose rows point most nearly the same way. First comes purple, with a score of 0.92, then white and black. Tom's neighbours are other names. Cat's are animals. Park's are places. A random pair of tokens scores only about 0.1, so these really are close.
segments.scene: Four real nearest-neighbour lists (cosine similarity over all 64 dims): 'red' → purple 0.92, white 0.85, black 0.84, yellow 0.75; 'tom' → max 0.63, finn 0.59, leo 0.58, zoe 0.58; 'cat' → bear 0.59, fish 0.57, dog 0.56, owl 0.54; 'park' → river 0.75, school 0.73, forest 0.71, house 0.71. Average token pair: 0.12.

segments.text: Now let's squash all 256 rows from 64 dimensions, one per number, down to two. We use a standard method called PCA, and plot each token as a dot. The names split off into their own island. Colors, animals, objects and places crowd together in one big group.
segments.scene: Real 2-D PCA of all 256 token embeddings (axes keep 12.6% of the variance). Names (teal) form a separate island at the bottom; colors, animals, objects and places bunch together on the right; other tokens are faint gray dots.

objects.label: 2-D PCA of the 256 real token embeddings (12.6% of variance)
the 12 name tokens (tom, mia, zoe, …) form their own island

10 animals tokens in the 2-D PCA map
10 objects tokens in the 2-D PCA map

segments.text: Let's zoom in. Re-run PCA on just these 48 words. The names sit far away. Colors and places get their own patches. Animals and objects overlap, and that makes sense: they fill the same slot in a sentence. They're nouns that come after 'the', and often after a color, like 'the red ball'. And in the full 64 dimensions, 48 out of 48 words have their nearest neighbour in their own group.

title: Attention, visually
subtitle: Queries, keys, values, softmax, the causal mask — and a real head that fetches a color

segments.text: How does the last word, 'the', find its way back to 'red'? The answer is attention. It lets each word look back at earlier words. Let's build it from three arrows.
segments.scene: The prompt start 'mia has a red ball' … 'tom has the' with a yellow curved arrow from the last ' the' back to ' red' and a question mark.

objects.label: the last token " the" (position 22)
token " red" (position 3)

segments.text: Every token, a chunk of text, carries a vector, a list of numbers. It turns that vector into three new ones. A query, which asks, what am I looking for? A key, which says, here's what I've got. And a value, the information it hands over if it gets picked. Each one comes from multiplying the vector by its own learned grid of numbers, called a matrix.
segments.scene: The token ' the' spawns three arrows: query (blue) 'what am I looking for?', key (teal) 'what do I contain?', value (orange) 'what do I hand over if picked?'. Note: each = the token's vector × its own learned matrix (W_Q, W_K, W_V).

objects.label: token " the" — its vector x feeds three learned matrices
query vector: what this token is looking for
key vector: what this token offers to be found by
value vector: the information it passes on
q = x·W_Q, k = x·W_K, v = x·W_V: three learned 64×16 matrices per head

segments.text: How well does a query match each earlier key? To score it, take the dot product: multiply the matching numbers, then add them up. Arrows pointing the same way score high. At right angles, the score is zero. Opposite arrows score negative.

segments.text: First, one small adjustment. Divide each score by the square root of the vector size. In this model, each attention unit is called a head. Each head uses keys of 16 numbers, so we divide by 4. This stops scores from growing just because the vectors are bigger. Big scores would push the next step, softmax, to extremes. Then softmax turns every score into a positive weight, and the weights add up to one. Here, red ends up with almost all the weight.

title: The MLP: where tokens think alone
subtitle: Expand, GELU, project back: real neurons in TinyGPT that detect patterns and push predictions

segments.text: Each layer of the model has two parts. Attention lets tokens, chunks of text, share information. Then every token goes off alone, through a small neural network called the MLP. It holds two thirds of each layer's weights, the numbers it learns.
segments.scene: One transformer layer: an attention box ('tokens share information') above an MLP box ('each token thinks alone'). A bar splits each layer's weights: attention 16,640 vs MLP 33,088 (67%).

MLP: processes each token's vector on its own

segments.text: Inside, there are three steps. First, expand the 64 numbers into 256 neurons, small units that each compute one number. Next, pass each through GELU, a simple curve that lets positive signals through and squashes negatives to nearly zero. Then project back down to 64, and add the result to the token's vector, its running list of numbers.
segments.scene: Network diagram: 64 inputs (blue) fan out to 256 hidden neurons (yellow; drawn 2 per dot) then back to 64 outputs (teal). Inset: the real GELU curve (negative in → ~0, positive in → passes). The output is added back to the token's vector.

Researchers have even changed facts a model states with one targeted edit to a single MLP layer. That's strong evidence, but not the whole story.

subtitle: How 256 raw scores become one word: softmax, temperature, top-k/top-p, greedy vs sampling

segments.text: How does a model pick its next word? It never outputs a word. Instead, it outputs 256 numbers. That's one score for every token, each small chunk of text it knows.
segments.scene: A wall of 256 thin bars — the model's real raw scores for every token in the vocab after the prompt; the tallest (pink) is ' red'.

objects.label: all 256 logits for the prompt (min -5.88, max 10.37)

segments.text: These raw scores are called logits, and higher means more likely. Our prompt ends with the words, now Tom has the. Red scores highest, at 10.4. White gets 7.7, and purple 7.5. Two thirds of all the tokens score below zero.
segments.scene: Bar chart of the six highest logits: ' red' 10.37, ' white' 7.68, ' purple' 7.53, ' black' 4.62, ' ava' 3.98, ',' 3.72; the other 250 range from 3.61 down to −5.88.

segments.text: Softmax then turns these scores into probabilities that add up to one. Raise e to the power of each logit, then divide each by their total. Those powers blow small gaps up into big ones. So red ends up with 87 percent, which means the model is quite sure.
segments.scene: The logit bars morph into probability bars: ' red' 87.1%, ' white' 5.9%, ' purple' 5.1%, ' black' 0.28%, ' ava' 0.15%, ',' 0.11%, all 250 others together 1.42%. Formula: p = exp(logit) / sum of exp over all 256 logits.

P(" purple") = 5.08% at T = 1
P(" black") = 0.28% at T = 1
all 250 other tokens together = 1.42% at T = 1

segments.text: Next comes a dial called temperature. It divides every logit before the softmax. Set to one, it changes nothing.
segments.scene: A big 'T = 1.0' dial appears top right and the formula gains '/ T': p = exp(logit / T) / sum of exp(all 256 logits / T); the bars stay at their T = 1 values.

segments.text: Weights are the numbers a model learns. Most start as tiny random noise. So at first, the model spreads its bets almost evenly over all 256 tokens, the chunks of text it can pick. Its loss, a score for how wrong its guesses are, is 5.56. That's almost exactly what pure guessing scores.

segments.text: Training is one simple game. At every position in the text, predict the next token. Each token on top points to the one that comes after it. The score is called cross-entropy: minus the log of the probability you gave the right answer. Lower is better.
segments.scene: Tokens of 'mia has a red ball.' on top, each with an arrow down to the token that follows it (the target). Formula: cross-entropy loss = −log(p[correct next token]).

title: Backprop: blame flows backwards
subtitle: The chain rule on a toy graph, then TinyGPT's real gradients for one prediction

segments.text: TinyGPT guessed red at 87 percent. That still leaves some loss, our score for how wrong it was. Which of its 170,560 weights, the numbers it learns, deserve the blame? And how much? Backpropagation, or backprop, answers that for all of them, in one sweep backwards.
segments.scene: The end of the probe prompt '… tom has the' → ' red' at 87.1%, loss 0.138; below, a grid of dots standing for the model's 170,560 weights with the question 'which ones are to blame?'.

objects.label: TinyGPT predicts " red" with p = 0.8707
cross-entropy loss = −ln(0.8707) = 0.1385
TinyGPT has 170,560 trainable weights (dots are a stand-in)

segments.text: Let's start with a toy version. Here, x is two, and w, the weight, is three. Going forward, two times three is six, plus one is seven. That misses the target, five, by two. Squared, the loss is four.
segments.scene: Toy computational graph (labelled toy): x = 2 and w = 3 feed a × node giving a = 6; a and b = 1 feed a + node giving z = 7; (z − t)² with target t = 5 gives loss L = 4. Forward values in teal.

objects.label: toy input x = 2
toy input w = 3
toy input b = 1
multiply node: a = w × x
add node: z = a + b
squared error node: L = (z − t)², target t = 5
forward value a = w·x = 6
forward value z = a + b = 7
toy loss L = (7 − 5)² = 4

segments.text: Now we go backwards, passing blame from the loss back to the inputs. The slope at z is how fast the loss changes when z moves. Here it's twice the miss: four. A plus node passes blame straight through. So a and b each get four. A times node scales the blame by the other input. So w gets eight, and x gets twelve.
segments.scene: Backward pass on the toy graph, arrows reversed, gradients in orange flowing right-to-left: ∂L/∂z = 2(z − 5) = 4; the + node copies it: ∂L/∂a = 4, ∂L/∂b = 4; the × node multiplies by the other input: ∂L/∂w = 4 × 2 = 8, ∂L/∂x = 4 × 3 = 12.

segments.text: Let's check that the brute-force way. Nudge w by a hair, a tiny amount, and the loss moves eight times as much. That's just what we predicted. So the rule is simple. Each node just multiplies the blame from above by its own local slope, and passes it on.
segments.scene: Finite-difference check of the toy gradient: (L(w+ε) − L(w−ε))/2ε with ε = 0.0001 gives 8.0000, matching ∂L/∂w = 8. Rule shown on top: blame in = blame from above × local slope.

segments.text: Now the real thing. The model gives each token, each possible next piece of text, a final score called a logit. Each logit's blame is its probability, minus one if it's the right answer. Red: minus 0.13, so push its score up. White and purple: plus, so push theirs down.

segments.text: That blame flows down through all three layers, from the output back to the input. Where paths merge, like the residual stream, blames add up. That stream is the running total that every layer adds to. From this one prediction, 167,744 weights get some blame, nearly all of them.

segments.text: Real training is different. It averages blame over each batch, a group of 4,096 predictions. It uses 0.003 only as the peak of a cosine schedule, which ramps the rate up, then down. And it lets AdamW, a smarter update rule, set each weight's step.

segments.text: Why does the backward pass cost about twice the forward pass? The model's main work is matrix multiplies, which combine big grids of numbers. Each forward matrix multiply needs two going back. It must work out blame for its inputs, and for its weights. So a training step costs roughly three forward passes.
segments.scene: Matrix diagram: forward Y = X·W (one multiply); backward dX = dY·Wᵀ (blame for inputs) and dW = Xᵀ·dY (blame for weights): two multiplies. Tally: forward ≈ 1, backward ≈ 2, training step ≈ 3 units (approximate). Note: activations must be stored for the backward pass.

backward: dX = dY·Wᵀ passes the gradient to the layer's input
backward: dW = Xᵀ·dY is the gradient for the weights
rule of thumb: backward ≈ 2× forward FLOPs, so a training step ≈ 3× a forward pass (approximate; depends on implementation)
backprop needs the forward activations, so training uses much more memory than inference

segments.text: Adam fixes this. For every weight, it keeps two running averages, updated every step. On top is the average of the gradient. That's the gradient, smoothed out, which is momentum. segments.scene: Adam's update: step = lr × avg(gradient) / √avg(gradient²). Top term = momentum (smoothed direction); bottom = each weight's own typical gradient size, so each weight moves at most about lr per step. PyTorch defaults β1 0.9, β2 0.999, + ε.

segments.text: Our real recipe for TinyGPT also changes the learning rate over time. That's called a schedule. First, warm up for 100 steps. title: Residuals & LayerNorm: why deep nets train
subtitle: Vanishing gradients, the residual highway, and what LayerNorm really rescales, with real ablations

segments.text: What lets deep networks train? Take every block of TinyGPT and delete its x plus, the part that adds the input back in. Train on the same data for the same 3,000 steps. The normal model gets its loss, the score for how wrong it is, down to 0.45. The edited one stalls at 4.50, about the unigram level: it only learned which words are common.
segments.scene: Code 'x = x + attn(LN(x))' with 'x +' struck out. Real validation curves, 3-layer TinyGPT trained 3000 steps: with residuals (teal) → 0.450; without (pink) stalls at 4.502, close to the unigram baseline 4.556 (dashed: a model that only knows word frequencies).

real: with residuals, final val loss 0.450
real: no residuals, final val loss 4.502 (stalled)
unigram baseline: cross-entropy 4.556 for a model that only knows word frequencies

segments.text: And the edited model ignores what you write. Give it three different prompts, and you get almost the same words back.
segments.scene: Real samples from the no-residual model for three different prompts: ' daym a. one the toam the a..ied pink no' | ' day hill a. one the toam the a..i\n. now' | ' daym a.ed say toam the a..ied. now.. bl'.

no-residual model, prompt …'q: what does the cat say? a:' → ' daym a.ed say toam the a..ied. now.. bl'

segments.text: So why does it break? To learn, training sends a gradient backward through every layer. The gradient tells each learned number which way to move. Without the plus, each layer multiplies it by its own slope, how strongly its output reacts to its input. In a deep stack without the plus, that means multiplying by about 0.2 at every layer. And twenty-four of those in a row leave almost nothing.
segments.scene: Backward pass as a chain of ×0.19 pills (the real average per-layer shrink of the gradient in a 24-layer no-residual TinyGPT at init); 0.19^24 = 4.0e-18.

objects.label: each layer multiplies the backward gradient by ~0.19 (real average, 24-layer probe)

segments.text: We measured this in a fresh 24-layer model, before any training. The x plus links are called residuals. And without residuals, the gradient reaching the first layer is 10 to the 17 times smaller than at the top, practically zero. Forward, from input to output, the signal keeps its size. But every position in the text ends up holding the same vector, the same list of numbers. With residuals, the gradient is nearly flat: the first layer gets about as much as the top.
segments.scene: Real measurement, a separate 24-layer TinyGPT at initialisation: RMS of the gradient reaching each layer (log scale). Without residuals (pink) it falls from 4.9e-04 at the top to 2.0e-21 at the input (×10^-17); with residuals (teal) it stays ≈ 5.5e-05–4.3e-05. Side note: without residuals the forward signal RMS stays 0.04–0.05, but positions become identical (spread 1.4e-07).

objects.label: real: gradient RMS without residuals, 4.92e-04 at the top layer → 1.98e-21 at the embeddings
without residuals the forward signal RMS stays 0.045–0.054 (LayerNorm rescales each block's input) but positions collapse: spread 1.4e-07 of the RMS at layer 24
real: gradient RMS with residuals, 4.33e-05 → 5.51e-05: nearly flat

segments.text: But our 3-layer model isn't that deep. Without the plus, its gradient shrinks only about 130 times. So how stuck it gets depends on the init, the random weights the model begins with. With the standard small init, it stalls. Start the blocks with larger weights, and the same stack, still without the plus, does learn. So residuals make depth easy to train, whatever the init.
segments.scene: Real: 3-layer TinyGPT without residuals at init, gradient shrinks 130× from top to embeddings. Two 600-step runs (batch 32): block init std 0.02 → val 4.569 (stalled), std 0.125 → 2.947 and still falling.

real: no residuals, std 0.02 init → val 4.569 after 600 steps
real: no residuals, std 0.125 init → val 2.947 after 600 steps

segments.text: So the plus sign builds a highway, called the residual stream. The signal travels straight along it, and each block reads from it and adds its own edit back. On the way back, during training, every plus passes the gradient through unchanged. So even the first layer gets a strong signal.
segments.scene: Diagram: a yellow 'residual stream' arrow left to right; attention and MLP blocks branch off it and add their output back through '+' nodes; a pink arrow below shows the gradient flowing straight back through every +.

objects.label: the residual stream: x passes straight through, blocks add to it
block reads the stream and adds its output back (x + f(x))
block reads the stream and adds its output back (x + f(x))
block reads the stream and adds its output back (x + f(x))
block reads the stream and adds its output back (x + f(x))
d(x + f(x))/dx = 1 + f'(x): the '1' carries gradient straight back

segments.text: But as blocks keep adding edits, the stream itself grows. This is where LayerNorm comes in. It doesn't shrink the stream. It hands each block a rescaled copy. It works on one token, one chunk of text, at a time. It subtracts the mean, the average of its numbers, and divides by their spread. Then a learned gain and bias adjust the result. So every block reads inputs of a sane size.
segments.scene: Illustration: a 12-number vector (orange, mean 0.7, std 1.5) passes through LayerNorm, (x − mean)/std (→ mean 0, std 1), then a learned gain and bias. Applied per token across its 64 numbers, to the copy each block reads; the residual stream itself is unchanged.

objects.label: illustrative vector before LayerNorm: mean 0.75, std 1.54
LayerNorm: (x − mean)/std, then × learned gain + bias
after normalising: mean 0, std 1; the learned gain and bias then rescale it
LayerNorm works per token over its 64 features, on the copy each block reads

segments.text: How much does this matter? In real trained 12-layer models, the stream grows about 12 times from bottom to top, even with LayerNorm. Without it, the stream grows 165 times. And the validation loss, measured on text kept out of training, ends at 0.69 instead of 0.62, so a bit worse. Remove the residuals instead, and it ends at 4.57, far worse.
segments.scene: Left: real RMS of the hidden state at each layer of trained 12-layer models: with LayerNorm 0.15 → 1.75; without 0.07 → 12.35. Right: real validation curves (1000 steps): residual+LN 0.620, no LN 0.693, no residual 4.569.

objects.label: real: signal RMS per layer with LayerNorm, 0.15 → 1.75
real: signal RMS per layer without LayerNorm, 0.07 → 12.35
real 12-layer run, residual + LN: final val loss 0.6202
real 12-layer run, no LN: final val loss 0.6934
real 12-layer run, no residual: final val loss 4.5686

segments.text: To sum up, every block is just two lines of code. Each line says the same thing: read a normalized copy, then add the result back. Virtually every modern transformer, the design TinyGPT uses, keeps both ideas. There's a residual stream that keeps gradients alive. And there's a normalization layer that keeps sizes sane, either LayerNorm or its simpler cousin RMSNorm.

Then it picks one, appends it, and repeats. GPT-family models, like those behind ChatGPT, run this same loop. And they're built from the same kinds of blocks.

segments.text: Stage two is supervised fine-tuning, an extra round of training. It uses the same loss, the score for how wrong the guesses are. But now it trains on example conversations written by people: a request, and a good response. The model learns to play the assistant.

segments.text: Stage three is preference tuning. People rank several answers to one prompt. From those rankings, a reward model learns their taste. It then scores the chat model's own answers, and reinforcement learning uses those scores. Learning by trial and reward, it nudges the chat model toward high reward, without drifting too far from its stage two version. That's RLHF: reinforcement learning from human feedback.

segments.text: Generating text has a speed trick: the KV cache. In attention, later tokens look back at each earlier token's key and value, the K and V. Those old keys and values never change, so keep them, and process only the newest position. For 8 new tokens, that's 30 positions instead of 212, with the same result.

segments.text: Then there are the sampling knobs, which control how the next token is picked. Temperature divides the logits, the raw scores, before they become probabilities. title: The research loop: test your own idea
subtitle: Hypothesis → smallest experiment → baseline → one change → compare → scale. A real TinyGPT experiment

segments.text: How do people invent a better model? It isn't one big idea. It's a loop. You start with a hypothesis, a guess you can test. Then you design the smallest experiment that could test it. You set up a baseline, the unchanged model to compare against. You make one change, and run an honest comparison. And only then do you scale up what wins. Let's run this loop, for real, on TinyGPT.
segments.scene: The research loop as six pills around a circle: hypothesis → smallest experiment → baseline → change ONE thing → compare across seeds → scale up what wins → back to hypothesis.

segments.text: Here's our hypothesis: TinyGPT doesn't need its position embeddings. Those are the numbers that tell each token, each small chunk of text, where it sits. Attention, where tokens look back at earlier ones, ignores word order by itself. But the causal mask, which hides every later token, leaks some. Each token sees a different number of tokens before it. So maybe the model can work out positions on its own.
segments.scene: TinyGPT's input = token embedding + position embedding, with the position embedding crossed out: 'what if TinyGPT had no position embeddings?'. A 6×6 causal mask: token k sees k tokens, so some order information leaks in.

segments.text: The smallest test is two short runs of 600 training steps, a few minutes at most on two CPU threads. Both use the same code, the same data and the same seed, the number behind the random start. They even see the same batches, the groups of examples trained on at each step. The baseline is unchanged TinyGPT, and the only difference is one line.

segments.text: Now, three classic traps. Different compute means unequal amounts of training. Compare against the released model, which trained five times longer, and the gap looks 7 times bigger than it really is. Unfair tuning: the learning rate, the size of each training step, was picked for the baseline, not for the variant. And leakage: 55 percent of the held-out lines, 39 percent of the text, also appear in the training data. So the model may have seen them before.

Data leakage: 1,642 of 3,001 held-out lines (54.7%) appear verbatim in the training split: all 1,579 short templated lines (Q&A, counting, pets, days, facts) but only 8 of 526 trade stories; 38.5% of held-out characters.

segments.text: Diffusion language models drop the left-to-right order. They start with every position masked, or hidden, and refine every position over a number of steps. Do they match the quality of autoregressive models, which write one token at a time like TinyGPT, at large scale? That's still open.

Open question: whether they match autoregressive quality and efficiency at scale is still being studied. Refs: D3PM (Austin et al. 2021) · masked diffusion LMs (e.g. Sahoo et al. 2024).

segments.text: Test-time compute means more thinking per question, at the moment of answering. The model can write out its reasoning steps, or produce several answers and take a vote. Some recent models are trained with reinforcement learning, learning by trial and reward, to reason longer.
segments.scene: Test-time compute & reasoning (changes how the generation loop is used in TinyGPT). Idea: spend more compute per question: write out steps, or sample several answers and vote. Open question: when extra thinking pays off, what it costs, and whether written steps reflect the real computation. Refs: chain of thought (Wei et al. 2022) · self-consistency (Wang et al. 2022) · DeepSeek-R1 (2025).

segments.text: And if you'd rather invent a better way to train, that's active too. People study optimizers, the rules for updating the learned numbers. They study data quality and curricula, the order data is taught in. Others try new objectives, like predicting several tokens at once, reinforcement learning after pretraining, or lower-precision math to save memory.

Open question: many reported gains shrink at larger scale or against a well-tuned baseline. Refs: Adam (Kingma & Ba 2015) · Micikevicius et al. 2018 · multi-token: Gloeckle et al. 2024.
